summary: Passports in Category A of the Guatemalan Institute of Migration's country classification (exempt from a visa) include those of Germany, the US, the UK, Canada, Australia and Japan; Guatemala's Migration Code says a tourist's stay may not exceed ninety days, extendable once. The UK Foreign Office says the 90-day period is shared with El Salvador and Nicaragua (the CA-4 Agreement also includes Honduras) and does not restart when you cross borders. Passports in Category B need a consular visa and those in Category C a consulted visa.

tips.text: The UK Foreign Office says you can travel between Guatemala, Nicaragua and El Salvador for up to 90 days without a visa (the CA-4 Agreement also includes Honduras), that the 90-day period starts when you enter any of these countries and does not restart when you cross borders, and that you can extend by up to 30 days by paying a fee before the 90 days expire.

The Instituto Guatemalteco de Migración charges USD 25 per application to extend a tourist or traveller visa, and says the application must be made before the authorised stay expires, otherwise you must pay a fine for irregular stay. The UK government says that if you overstay the 90 days you will have to pay a fine before leaving the country.

The UK Foreign Office says PROATUR, the tourist assistance and emergency service of INGUAT, provides 24-hour emergency assistance and routine guidance to tourists, with call centre staff who speak English and Spanish: call +502 2290 2810, or 1500 from inside Guatemala.

The UK Foreign Office says some volcanoes are at high altitude with freezing temperatures at night, that local tour organisers tend to underestimate the risks and deaths have occurred, and that there is no mountain rescue service. It says to check the websites of the Guatemalan Meteorological Office and CONRED for access, restrictions and recommendations before you climb.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Guatemala?
faq.answer: Category A of the Guatemalan Institute of Migration's country classification is exempt from a visa; it includes Germany, the US, the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Japan, and the UK Foreign Office says British nationals can visit for up to 90 days without a visa. Passports in Category B need a consular visa and those in Category C a consulted visa.

faq.question: How does the CA-4 90-day rule work in Guatemala?
faq.answer: The UK Foreign Office says you can travel between Guatemala, Nicaragua and El Salvador for up to 90 days without a visa, and that the CA-4 Agreement also includes Honduras, for which British nationals need a visa. It says the 90-day period starts when you enter any of these countries and does not restart when you cross borders, and that you can extend your stay by up to 30 days by paying a fee before the 90 days expire.

faq.question: Can I do a border run to reset my 90 days?
faq.answer: Not by crossing between the CA-4 countries: the UK Foreign Office says the 90-day period starts when you enter Guatemala, Nicaragua or El Salvador and does not restart when you cross borders. It says you can extend your stay by up to 30 days by paying a fee before the 90 days expire.

faq.question: Is Guatemala safe for tourists?
faq.answer: The UK Foreign Office says Guatemala has one of the highest violent crime rates in Latin America, and that there have been armed attacks or robberies on most tourist routes between Guatemala City, Antigua, Tikal, Petén and Lake Atitlán. It says to avoid travelling on public buses (repainted US school buses), that for shorter trips within towns the safest option is radio-dispatched taxis, Uber or hotel taxis, and that PROATUR, Guatemala's tourist assistance service, can be reached on 1500 from inside Guatemala.

faq.question: What money should I use in Guatemala?
faq.answer: No official source we could read describes card acceptance. The UK Foreign Office says it is often not possible to exchange British pounds in Guatemala and much easier to exchange US dollars, to check ATMs for evidence of tampering, and that it is safer to change money in hotels, at banks or at foreign exchange offices.
